528841cbf861a044: Most staples for Thanksgiving, including potatoes and cranberries, haven't jumped in price this year. Noah Samuel Franz on UnsplashInflation-weary Americans have at least some good news to cheer this holiday season: The cost of a basic Thanksgiving meal has stabilized. A Thanksgiving dinner for 10 people clocks in at US$78.93, approximately 0.4% less than in 2025, according to the Wells Fargo Agri-Food Institute. That’s because most staples haven’t seen a sharp jump in prices. Americans are still justified in feeling stressed about high grocery bills, but it’s because of the cumulative effect of rising prices in recent years. While inflation has slowed since its peak of more than 9% in 2022, the cost of a Thanksgiving meal is roughly 25% higher than it was before the COVID-19 pandemic began. I’m an agricultural economist who has been studying the many drivers of food inflation. What’s key to remember is that inflation data tells us how quickly prices are increasing, not whether prices are returning to previous levels. So even modest price jumps today are layered on already-elevated prices. Here’s what Americans can expect when they go shopping for Thanksgiving, from turkey to dessert: Go for frozen turkey Stable frozen turkey prices have played an important role in keeping overall holiday meal costs close to last year’s levels. The average advertised price for a frozen turkey over 16 pounds (about 7 kilograms) was $0.96 per pound, essentially unchanged from the $0.97 per pound in the same period last year, according to the USDA Agricultural Marketing Service’s Weekly Turkey Report, published on Nov. 13, 2026. These prices reflect the typical discounts leading up to Thanksgiving, when retailers often cut turkey prices as part of their holiday promotions. It’s a different story with fresh turkey prices, which are about 11% higher than a year ago, according to the Department of Agriculture data. So shoppers seeking a fresh bird may face a higher grocery bill. A longer-term trend is that turkey consumption has gradually declined over time. As a result, the cost of Thanksgiving depends on much more than turkey prices alone. This is where side dishes come in. Frozen turkey is among the Thanksgiving staples that haven’t seen big price jumps this past year. AP Photo/Nam Y. Huh A mixed picture for side dishes Mashed potatoes, cranberry sauce and sweet potato casserole are among the dishes that a frugal shopper might consider. Sweet potatoes are 12.5% cheaper year on year, and cranberry prices have dropped 4.8%, according to the USDA Agricultural Marketing Service’s Weekly Grocery Store Specialty Crops data. Potato prices, meanwhile, have been stable, increasing just 1.1% over the past year, according to September’s consumer price index, the most recent month of full data. If you’re considering mac and cheese, the costs of the main ingredients should balance out: Pasta and cornmeal prices are 4.3% higher year on year, while cheese is 3% cheaper. Prices for fruits and vegetables, however, have mostly ticked upward and are 3.9% higher than a year ago. That includes green beans, which are 2.2% more expensive. Prices for fresh apples are up 7.5%, and up 2.6% for lettuce. More broadly, higher prices for some fresh vegetables reflect the cost pressures facing food production. Farmers are grappling with high fertilizer, fuel and transportation expenses, not to mention tariffs in certain sectors. Of course, Thanksgiving isn’t complete without regional traditions. Sauerkraut is a popular side dish for turkey in the mid-Atlantic states, but fans will have to pay substantially more. Cabbage is about 30% more expensive year on year due to weather shocks and pest outbreaks that have reduced supply. Sauerkraut, a popular side dish in mid-Atlantic states, is likely to be pricier amid higher cabbage prices. Kelsey Todd on Unsplash Don’t forget dessert Americans might also find some sweet relief in prices for popular desserts. Some key baking staples became more affordable. Butter prices have fallen 10.3% over the previous year, while flour is down by 1.1% and sugar by 1%, according to the September consumer price index data. But some of the biggest savings come from eggs, where prices have dropped sharply. Like the turkey industry, egg production was hard-hit in 2022 by a highly pathogenic avian flu outbreak, which reduced supplies and pushed prices up. Since then, producers have rebuilt flocks and expanded production to grow supply. Egg prices are now 20.3% lower than a year ago. Where consumers will shell out more is milk, up 2.3%; canned fruit, up 2.3%; and frozen bakery products, up 1.3%, according to the consumer price index data. Pumpkins for pie-making will cost 2% more than last year. So keep all this in mind if you plan to bake a pie. And if you opt for a store-bought pumpkin pie, expect to pay about 2.5% more. Where other savings can be found Shoppers looking for alternatives to turkey could head to the poultry aisle. Prices for whole fryer and roaster chickens are anywhere from 7% to 20% lower than a year ago, according to USDA grocery store price data. Consumers can also take advantage of Thanksgiving promotions offered by grocery retailers. Several major retailers offer complete Thanksgiving meal baskets for less than $40, which can translate to approximately $3.50 to $4 per person. Among major retailers, Walmart is advertising its Thanksgiving basket for 10 people at $35, Aldi at $39 for 10 people and Target at $30 for six people. Although the contents vary, these meal packages generally include Thanksgiving favorites such as turkey, stuffing and cranberry sauce, and ingredients for green bean and potato side dishes. Inflation remains at the top of consumers’ minds, and it isn’t expected to ease anytime soon. But in the case of Thanksgiving, shoppers can find at least some relief as they seek out staples for their feast. Elizabeth Canales receives funding from the U.S. Department of Agriculture and the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.
c1253c89a3ee647b: Microsoft has pushed Windows Server 2028 into public preview, with an eye on beefed-up security, new infrastructure support, and the inevitable nod to AI.

Neil Hinnant, a director on the Windows Server team, talked up the security tweaks. There's a hardened Server Core configuration by default and a new security baseline. "Trusted Launch extends protection to virtual machines," he wrote. "Confidential VM support begins a journey to support integrity-protected runtimes on supported CVM hardware."
Server Core will therefore arrive locked down by default – good news for security, potentially less so for administrators whose existing configurations depend on more permissive settings.

"For years, Windows Server shipped compatible by default," wrote Senior Product Manager Christina Curlette. "Making the server secure was up to you, usually by applying the Security Baseline or your own hardening scripts after setup."

With Windows Server 2028 (and starting from Windows Server Insider Preview build 29706), Server Core will be installed hardened. "Hundreds of security settings are on from first boot," Curlette wrote.

"Because the defaults are now locked down, some things that worked on Windows Server 2025 may not work on Windows Server 2028 without changes. This includes older protocols, legacy authentication, and some management tools and scripts."

For a company obsessed with backward compatibility, this is quite the step. Welcome though the hardening is, administrators will need to test carefully: working on Windows Server 2025 won't guarantee a smooth ride in the brave new world.

AI gets a role on both sides of the security fence: helping uncover vulnerabilities and giving Microsoft another reason to sell servers. Windows Server 2028 is being pitched for running models locally, with support for accelerators such as AMD's Instinct MI350P.

Not every server is destined to babysit a model, however, and the storage changes may be more immediately useful to enterprise administrators. Windows Server 2028 will enable native NVMe storage by default, along with NVMe over TCP and RDMA. Booting from ReFS is also planned, adding another item to the storage upgrade list.

Intune management for Windows Server has also entered preview. Azure Arc, with its cloud-native management workflows, is obviously still around, while Intune brings a more familiar management interface for administrators already using it for endpoints.

Hinnant acknowledged that this was a "major release," and it looks like the security hardening alone will require a good deal of thought from administrators before organizations adopt the eventual production release.

Esben Dochy, Principal Technical Evangelist for SecOps at Lansweeper, told The Register that Microsoft had indicated that the hardened security only applied to new installations. "If that remains in the final release," he said, "in-place upgrades could be easier. The catch is that those servers may also miss out on the new security defaults."
"Hardening is the right direction," he said, "but it will add work for teams moving to Server 2028."

According to Lansweeper’s figures, as of October 2026, Windows Server 2019 ruled the roost with 33 percent. Windows Server 2025 had reached just 7 percent. "From behavior we've seen in the past," said Dochy, "adoption is primarily driven by lifecycle, so until the more used versions start going EOL, I don't expect much adoption, similar to what Server 2025 is experiencing."

Windows Server 2025 remains under extended support until 2034, but Microsoft's direction of travel is clear: beefed-up security by default, a home for AI applications, and Intune management for fleets of servers. ®
62b49bc7f7abf6f9: This is today’s edition of The Download, our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what’s going on in the world of technology.
This smell startup says its AI nose is as good as a human’s

In a New Jersey lab, researchers are trying to sniff every odor on Earth. Their careful notes—“nutty,” “peachy,” “marine”—are cross-referenced with chemical analyses to train what AI startup Osmo calls the world’s first foundation model for smell. Its goal, says founder Alex Wiltschko, is “to give computers a sense of smell.”

Wiltschko claims the model has already achieved “human-level olfactory intelligence” and is helping fragrance brands design new scents. But Osmo has bigger ambitions, from detecting counterfeit goods to diagnosing diseases. Not everyone is convinced its technology can deliver.
How far could an AI-powered sense of smell really take us?

Hydropower hit record lows in the US Southwest this summer
The US Southwest generated 28% less electricity via hydropower between April and August than the 10-year average, according to new data from the US Energy Information Administration.

Most hydropower plants in the US rely on dams to hold back water, creating reservoirs. But an extreme, prolonged drought has left water levels dangerously low in the region’s two largest reservoirs—and climate change is adding to the pressure.

Transformers are a crucial but nearly invisible part of the US grid, helping move power efficiently across long distances. But they’re complicated and in short supply, and their basic design hasn’t changed much in about a century.

bc49214a83160d25: SHENZHEN, Nov 18 — At a park refreshment stand in China’s tech capital Shenzhen, a humanoid robot grabs a cup and pulls a lever to form an ice-cream spiral, then hands the customer their order. It’s the kind of futuristic scene the country is keen to showcase as world leaders including Donald Trump and Vladimir Putin head to Shenzhen, a manufacturing hub north of Hong Kong, for this week’s Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit. Chinese robots are famous for their slick dance moves, but artificial intelligence engineers are trying to train them up to join the workforce – using reams of data captured by humans in headcams to help hone the machines’ skills. Although they still struggle with complex tasks like cleaning or ironing on their own, robots are already taking on more simple roles across the country. “Mum, look!” a girl exclaimed when she spotted the ice-cream humanoid and its colleague that makes coffee – treats on sale for around US$4 (RM16) each – as passersby film the spectacle on their phones. The startup said 200 of its humanoid servers are deployed in China, and up to 300 coffees are sold each day in the Shenzhen park. “We’re getting data feedback from many real scenarios,” said CEO Guo Yandong, such as different light conditions that could help robots adapt to unpredictable environments. ‘Workshop of the world’ In China, 83 percent of people surveyed by Ipsos this year said they were excited by products and services that use AI, the highest of 32 countries including the United States, where just a third of people agreed with the statement. At battery giant CATL, humanoids made by China’s Spirit AI already take the dangerous job of plugging in high-voltage connectors. Strange Attractor’s Kang foresees a “massive deployment” of AI-powered robots in China next year. Some could pick strawberries, or help with housework – “but for sure, it’s not gonna be that intelligent, it’s just the start.” — AFP
c73f0e8efc68f162: TOKYO, Nov 18 — Japan’s longest-serving coach Hajime Moriyasu leaves a mixed legacy after the curtain fell on his eight-year reign, with historic wins offset by a lack of trophies. Moriyasu led Japan to shock wins over Germany and Spain at the 2022 World Cup in Qatar and he also engineered first victories over Brazil and England in friendlies. Great expectations Osumi said Moriyasu helped create an identity for Japanese football that has taken root right across the board. “He built a foundation so that the team could press from the front and help each other in defence and never slack off,” he said. “That has become established not just in the full national team but also in the age-level teams and the women’s teams.” Japanese media reported that Moriyasu could now return to the J. League or try his luck overseas. Belgium’s Sint-Truiden, who have Japanese owners and have given several Japanese players a gateway into Europe, have been mentioned as a possible destination. The journalist Mori believes the self-effacing Moriyasu could need “more of an ego” to succeed in Europe. “When restrictions were placed on who he could call up, with scheduling issues and so on, a normal coach would probably complain that their needs should take priority,” said Mori. “But Moriyasu would accept everything, saying he’d do his best within the rules that had been set.” Oiwa, a former international defender who has led Japan’s Under-23s since 2021, is known to have a similar approach to Moriyasu. Mori believes the new man can take the team to the next level. “Using the rich soil that Moriyasu has cultivated for the past eight years, I think Oiwa will have a more aggressive, results-based style aimed at getting Japan to the World Cup quarter-finals and beyond,” he said. — AFP
df0acd98824586e8: BANGKOK, Nov 18 — Chemicals found almost everywhere in modern life pose a “global and growing threat” to human health and the environment, a landmark report based on over a decade of research has warned. The report on “endocrine-disrupting chemicals” (EDCs) released by the United Nations Environment Programme and World Health Organization “conservatively” estimates the health and environmental costs of EDC exposure at over US$1 trillion (RM4.1 trillion) annually. “The scientific evidence is clear: EDCs are a global and growing threat to human and environmental health,” warns the report written by international scientists, calling current regulations “uneven and insufficient.” EDCs are chemicals that interfere with, mimic, or block the hormones that regulate the development and behaviour of our organs. They are in everything from toys and makeup, to building materials and clothing. The report released late Tuesday is the first such comprehensive look at EDC impacts in 14 years, and finds increasingly clear links between them and a range of diseases. “The evidence is so strong that it’s irrefutable at this point,” said Laura Vandenberg, report co-author and professor of environmental health sciences at the University of Massachusetts Amherst. The report examined thousands of studies on chemicals like bisphenols, phthalates and parabens. Evidence of links between these chemicals and disease is strongest for certain neurological conditions and reproductive problems including sperm decline. But there is also growing confidence that EDCs are linked to diseases like type 2 diabetes and asthma that have spiked globally. “Because these changes are occurring rapidly, they are unlikely to be explained primarily by genetic change,” the report says. ‘Sufficiently worrisome’ Scientists looked at associations between EDC exposure and health conditions, as well as the mechanisms by which exposure could cause harm. The findings vary, with “strong evidence” of developmental and neurobehavioral effects, but “emerging” links between EDCs and cardiovascular disease. However, the overall risk is strong because EDCs are so ubiquitous and likely to impact health at tiny levels, Vandenberg said. Among those most at risk are workers in the chemicals and recycling industries, particularly in countries with weak regulations. A 2024 study by the International Pollutants Elimination Network NGO fitted participants with silicone wristbands that absorbed chemicals. Lab tests of the wristbands found that plastic waste and recycling workers in Thailand and Kenya were exposed to over 20 hazardous chemicals, while even control subjects working in offices were exposed to at least 11. There are around 1,000 identified EDCs, but experts say many chemicals have simply not been tested properly and their impacts remain unknown. They are also concerned about “synergistic” impacts — the way exposure to multiple chemicals may amplify health effects. The “proverbial million-dollar question” is what level of EDC exposure triggers any given health impact, said Frederic Leusch, professor of environmental toxicology at Australia’s Griffith University, who was not involved in the report. But even absent an answer, Leusch believes “the hazard is sufficiently worrisome that we need to take action to reduce our, and our environment’s, exposure.” ‘It scares politicians’ Many countries have regulated certain EDCs, often targeting bisphenol A, particularly in children’s products. But regulators have struggled to determine which chemicals should be regulated, and what an appropriate exposure level might be. “It scares politicians, to some extent, because it’s such a complicated area,” said retired professor of environmental chemistry Ake Bergman, who worked on the previous editions of the EDC report in 2002 and 2012. Like other experts, he warned there is no known safe exposure level for most EDCs. “We have some that are really acting at extremely low concentrations.” In a statement, the International Council of Chemical Associations industry group called for “science-based” approaches to regulation that protect health and the environment “while enabling society to benefit from the products, technologies, and innovations that are essential to modern life and sustainable development.” Many EDCs are in plastics, and experts say oil firms are increasing plastic production as demand for fossil fuel energy falls. “We need to stop the expansion of plastic production,... reduce exposures to EDCs, and ban the worst actors,” said Tracey Woodruff, report co-author and professor at Stanford University. “While more science is always needed, we don’t need more science to act.” — AFP

923ebe5486798a7b: BUDAPEST: Leaked Deutsche Bank documents reveal that a suspected Russian money-laundering network funnelled money through a Hungarian bank owned by allies of the country's ex-leader Viktor Orban, Hungarian media reported Wednesday.

International media, including The Financial Times, Le Monde and The New York Times, published reports Tuesday based on millions of leaked documents and emails that shine a light on questionable past practices at the German banking giant.
The media consortium found that several major companies involved were linked to the sanctioned Russian oligarch Oleg Deripaska.
The documents show that MKB, a bank partly owned by the Hungarian government, played a key role in a suspected Russian "laundromat" network, the investigative site Direkt36 said.

MKB came under the control of businessmen closely tied to Orban, the Kremlin-friendly prime minister at the time, in 2017 and later helped finance his far-right allies abroad, including France's Marine Le Pen.
The Russian network transferred at least €1.7 billion (US$1.9 million) between 2017 and 2020 and displayed "numerous signs of organised crime", according to Direkt36.
"MKB Bank played a key role in the network's operation, having initiated and received the highest proportion of transfers," Direkt36 said.
Five of the network's 15 key companies, which were mostly registered in Hong Kong and Cyprus, held accounts at the bank despite having no apparent connection to Hungary, it added.
"These had received and sent at least €460 million," the report said.

Although MKB claimed it had closed most of its offshore client accounts in 2019, Deutsche Bank did not see a "significant" decrease in "the high proportion of transactions originating from non-resident clients", according to the article.

This led the German banking giant to sever its longstanding relationship with the Hungarian bank, which caused a brief "panic" at MKB until it secured a replacement arrangement with the Dutch bank ING, Direkt36 said.
MKB and its successor MBH Bank have come under media scrutiny in Hungary for financing projects linked to Orban's allies.

Austrian media on Wednesday also reported that documents from the Deutsche Bank leak showed payments from a suspected money-laundering network to several Austrian companies, including the private jet operator Avcon Jet and helicopter services provider Wucher.
One of the network's Hong Kong-registered companies, Dempshire Corporation, had ties to Deripaska and channelled more than €130 million over three years, Der Standard reported.
a73424645a5daf48: Fifteen people have been arrested over an alleged scam that squeezed more money from investment fraud victims by offering to help recover their losses.

City of London Police searched 17 London addresses on November 11 and apprehended 14 men and one woman. All have since been released on bail. Investigators say the suspected fraudsters posed as regulators to persuade previous victims that compensation was available.
Reports submitted through the UK's Report Fraud service helped investigators trace the compensation pitch to around 3,000 recipients since October 2025.
Most victims were elderly, police said. The offers arrived by letter and email, promising redress for earlier investment losses.

City of London Police said the victims were initially targeted by a range of investment scams related to art, carbon credits, land, whisky, wine, and pensions, and that some took place more than a decade prior to their re-victimization.
Targets were directed to a company that demanded a holding fee before supposedly reclaiming their money. Police say those who paid were left further out of pocket.

"Today's action sends a clear message to those who target vulnerable people for financial gain: you will be pursued and will face robust action," said Nik Adams, deputy commissioner at the City of London Police.
"Behind every fraud report is a real person whose trust has been damaged, and in some cases, whose life savings have been stolen. We know the impact of these crimes can be devastating.

"This case highlights the importance of reporting fraud through the Report Fraud service. Information provided by victims helped investigators link reports together, uncover the wider conspiracy, and identify those involved. It is a powerful reminder that every report counts and can play a vital role in bringing offenders to justice."
The investigation also extends beyond London, with police identifying locations linked to the case in Kent and Hertfordshire.
The searches resulted in officers seizing cash, drugs, and other high-value items, including a watch worth around £230,000, with the total haul valued at more than £2 million.
Police put losses identified so far at £1.5 million and expect that figure to rise as the investigation continues.
Knowing the details of an earlier scam doesn't make a caller trustworthy, police warned. That information can be used to sell victims a second fraud.
Report Fraud has also highlighted substantial losses in other scams affecting older people.

Fraudsters exploiting positions of trust stole a reported £93.8 million during 2025/26. People aged 70 and over lost more than £51 million, with relatives, friends, carers, and others entrusted with their finances among the perpetrators. Report Fraud received 3,812 reports in this category.
"The impact of fraud extends far beyond financial loss, especially when it is carried out by those who are trusted by the victim," said Mark Evans, president at the Law Society of England and Wales.

Similarly, at the end of October, Report Fraud said £24.3 million was stolen between January and August 2026 through AI-augmented investment scams, with people aged 60 and over accounting for nearly 80 percent of reports.
However, it's not always the elderly in scammers' crosshairs. Those in the 30-39 age bracket accounted for the most reports in one of the most lucrative frauds affecting Brits in recent times.

Payment diversion fraud, which tricks victims into paying a criminal's bank account instead of the intended recipient's, resulted in £101 million in losses in the 2025/26 financial year, according to Report Fraud's figures. ®
48c3827e858de6ee: In the one light-day that humanity's most distant object has now traveled from Earth, there has been enough time for details about its creation—and what it left behind—to be discovered again.

Voyager 1, which left Earth in 1977 on an initial mission to fly by Jupiter and Saturn (as well as the latter's moon Titan), crossed into interstellar space in 2012. Like its twin (Voyager 2), Voyager 1 carries a "commemorative phonograph record," in part as a nod to the 100th anniversary of the recording medium and as a message from humanity to whoever (or whatever) encounters the spacecraft on its journey through outer space.

About those forgotten bits, ask Glen Swanson. While researching the history of the Golden Record, he uncovered the discs' overlooked second set of operating directions and located the duplicates that were made and distributed almost five decades ago.

69c36030a7446a10: PARIS، Nov 18 —After 13 years of waiting، including two delays and several leaks، the first gamers began playing Wednesday the latest instalment of Grand Theft Auto، the most expensive — and among the most profitable — video game ever developed. GTA VI becomes available on PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series consoles at midnight Thursday in each region where it will be available. That meant it launched first in New Zealand (at 1100 GMT on Wednesday)، with many players around the world changing their console location settings to the far-eastern country to be among the first to enter the new Vice City. “I’ve been playing GTA for such a long time that the anticipation for this is crazy، ” Australian student Riley Fennel told AFP ahead of the launch. Although Rockstar Games، the studio behind GTA، has not yet released advance unit sales figures، specialist firm Sensor Tower estimates they have already surpassed 15 million. That would be more than US$1.5 billion (RM6.17 billion) in revenue before the game even came out، for a budget estimated at US$1 billion to US$1.5 billion، which would be unprecedented. According to the British analytics firm Omdia، sales of GTA VI could reach US$3.2 billion by the end of the year. ‘Taylor Swift of games’ “No other concert or box office release has ever generated that much capital. And so that makes it one of the outliers in entertainment، ” said Joost van Dreunen، a professor at New York University’s Stern School of Business. “This is the Taylor Swift of video games، ” the industry specialist said. Rockstar’s parent company، US publisher Take-Two Interactive، has rolled out a massive marketing campaign to establish the title as a mass cultural product that transcends the boundaries of video games. “The reach of the game is such that it will lead to a downstream effect on engagement on other entertainment services، ” such as streaming platforms، said James McWhirter at Omdia. “I’m going to take four days off، ” said Dmytro Shkambara، a 27-year-old Ukrainian player living in Berlin، who said he had been planning this first game session “for a very long time”. Like him، many fans have already booked time off to immerse themselves in the fictional state of Leonida، inspired by Florida. The human resources platform Remote said it had seen a 32 percent increase in leave requests around the world for November 19. Touted as bigger، better and more realistic than its predecessors، “GTA VI” follows the adventures of a Bonnie-and-Clyde-style couple trying to survive in the Miami-inspired، crime-ravaged Vice City. Since its beginnings، the series has won players over with its increasingly realistic reconstructions of fictionalised cities and the great freedom of action offered in a highly detailed open world. Gamers entering GTA’s worlds can drive cars، fly planes or go skydiving. “GTA VI” promises to push its realism even further، with characters looking different depending on what they eat and players having to work at cultivating the relationship between the protagonists. Ahead of its release، the game picked up eight nominations on Tuesday at the Game Awards، the American ceremony that will honour the best video games of the year on December 10. Subversion and controversy Rockstar، which by 2026 will have a dozen studios around the world and more than 4,700 employees، devoted more than eight years to building the latest GTA instalment. Active production only began after the release of Rockstar’s previous game، “Red Dead Redemption II”، in 2018. It was a rocky ride to release. Shaken by a series of leaks in 2022 and the online release of stolen gameplay videos، the studio postponed the launch twice، then suffered a new round of leaks last summer. The games have also regularly been accused of glorifying violence and illegal behaviour as GTA has carved out a place in pop culture as a symbol of subversion، unafraid to mock the flaws of American society. Players can run over pedestrians، sell drugs and shoot at the police. “It’s a series that is famous for being always over the top in terms of its representation of violence and different forms of abuse or harassment، for its representations of gender”، said Paolo Ruffino، a lecturer in digital cultures at King’s College London. “I don’t expect to see necessarily major controversies unless there is something completely new، ” he added. But as a consequence of its scandalous legacy، several countries have banned the saga. No official release is currently planned in Russia، China، Lebanon or Qatar. — AFP
032e2c1fabfc0abb: BANGKOK: A Thai minister on Wednesday contradicted Donald Trump's characterisation of a bilateral trade agreement as eliminating all tariffs, saying the US president was putting a positive spin on it for American voters.
Trump had announced that "Thailand will eliminate all tariffs on US exports" as he signed a joint statement with Thai Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul during a summit in Manila on Tuesday.
Commerce Minister Suphajee Suthumpun told reporters that was not the case and "Thailand has not agreed to eliminate all tariffs on US imports, contrary to comments made by Donald Trump."
"Nor will Thailand immediately open its market completely or allow 100%t liberalised trade from the outset," Suphajee added.
"President Trump likely wanted Americans to hear a positive message, which is why he framed the agreement in that way," she said.
The US is Thailand's largest export market, with the Southeast Asian nation recording a surplus of US$71.7 billion last year, according to US data.
It has been buffeted by Trump's tariff hikes, with the most recent announced in July standing at 12.5%.
Thailand was also included this week among countries subject to new US export licences on advanced AI chips, intended to prevent Chinese firms from obtaining access to the technology.

Last year, Thailand and the US agreed on a framework for reciprocal trade that would see Thailand remove "tariffs on 99% of goods", while the US would seek to maintain a baseline 19% rate for Thai imports, Washington said.

Under the final agreement, which has not yet been signed, "market access will be phased in gradually, as there remain a number of sensitive products that require special consideration, including certain agricultural goods," Suphajee said.

Washington announced the trade framework with Thailand alongside a similar deal with Cambodia in October 2025, on the same day that Trump co-signed a ceasefire agreement between the two neighbours involved in deadly border clashes.
The timing prompted speculation Trump had used US economic ties as leverage to try to end the conflict -- one of several he says he has solved.

53bf28c36494803d: The activist admits his mental state has been negatively affected by the 10-year sentence increase
Originally published on Global Voices
Joshua Wong released from Lai Chi Kok Reception Centre on June 17, 2019. HKFP's File photo.

This article was originally published by Hong Kong Free Press on November 16, 2026. The following version is edited and republished on Global Voices under a content partnership agreement. It is also part of Global Voices’ November 2026 Spotlight series, “Justice as infrastructure.” You can support this coverage by donating here.

In a letter from a Hong Kong prison earlier this year, jailed activist Joshua Wong expressed dread over the looming sentence in his foreign collusion case. “Fretting about whether it’s 2032 or 2037, my mental state is hardly all right,” he wrote in Chinese, weighing when he might regain his freedom.
The agony inevitably stems from this: What if it’s 2037? Well, it’s easy [for people] to sympathise in the moment, but it’s difficult to be consistent, and it will only get harder.

The 30-year-old pro-democracy activist has already spent almost six years behind bars over various offences and was set for release in January 2026, until authorities charged him last year with conspiring to collude with foreign forces — the second case against him under the Beijing-imposed national security law. His case is one of the most high-profile examples of changing judicial norms in Hong Kong.
A prison letter Joshua Wong wrote to friend and former fellow student activist Louis Lee in February 2026. This photo was taken on September 30, 2026. Photo by Kyle Lam/HKFP. Used with permission.

On November 5, just two months before he was due to be released, a court sentenced him to 10 more years in prison for colluding with foreign forces. He is now expected to serve until late 2036, when he turns 40.

Standing in the courtroom as his new sentence was announced, Wong shook his head slightly and made notes, but appeared calm. Judge William Tam ruled that Wong’s offence was one of a “grave nature” under the national security law, which carries a minimum penalty of 10 years in jail and up to life imprisonment.
The judge knocked off three years from a 13-year starting sentence for Wong’s guilty plea.

In prison correspondence shared with HKFP by two close friends ahead of Wong’s sentencing, the former poster child of Hong Kong’s democracy movement had at times reflected on the weight of facing an additional decade behind bars. He expressed anxiety over fading from the memory of his friends — and from society at large. In one letter, Wong wrote:
I have no idea how much more I will lose in the passing of time. Responsibility is, in fact, response-ability. But who will respond? I can’t help but ponder and doubt.

Once a pro-democracy activist dedicated first and foremost to Hong Kong’s political future, Wong began campaigning as a charismatic, eloquent student leader who dared to stand up to the authorities — even to Beijing. Hong Kong is an overseas territory of China, and has increasingly been pressured to conform to China’s political goals in recent years, despite agreements that Hong Kong would retain “a high degree of autonomy” when handed over to China in 1997. A Netflix documentary about him is succinctly titled “Joshua: Teenager vs. Superpower.”

Yet, after years behind bars, Wong has changed. The teenager who focused single-mindedly on Hong Kong’s democracy movement has become even more caring for those around him despite being separated by prison walls, according to his friends.
Tiffany Chin, a former student activist who campaigned alongside Wong, said. The pair were once romantically involved and are now friends. She shared:
For me, it doesn’t feel like we’re the only ones supporting him. In fact, he has been supporting people on the outside in his own way.
And, with the political causes he once championed now firmly crushed, Wong has turned inward to reflect on himself. In another letter, he wrote:
We had held such high aspirations for society from a young age, we should hold ourselves to the same standard. Only by refusing a life of mediocrity can we be worthy of the world we envisioned.
From “robot” to caring friend

On a bright summer day in June 2025, while serving a sentence for subversion at Stanley Prison, Wong was arrested behind bars and brought to court the same day on a fresh charge of conspiracy to collude with foreign forces.
The prosecution came without warning. That day, Chin and Louis Lee, another longtime friend of Wong’s, rushed to the court after hearing the news, but failed to see him in person.

Authorities accused him of conspiring with Nathan Law — another high-profile, pro-democracy student activist — in 2020 to collude with foreign elements, citing Wong’s sharing of Law’s social media posts calling for international sanctions against Hong Kong as evidence.
The unexpected new charge was devastating to Wong. That month, he confessed he was under a lot of pressure — a vulnerability he rarely showed in the past, Chin said.

After so many prison terms and all the ups and downs over the last decade… he seldom openly showed vulnerability. So when he felt the need to say so bluntly that he was not OK, I truly believed he wasn’t.

Having begun campaigning at the age of 14, Wong has been in and out of prison throughout his years of activism. He now has a total of eight criminal convictions, including three separate offences linked to unlawful assembly and two national security offences.
Joshua Wong is photographed inside the Lai Chi Kwok Reception Centre on March 4, 2021. Photo via HKFP. Used with permission.

Born in 1996 to a Christian family – one year before Hong Kong was handed over to China from British rule – Wong rose to prominence in 2011 when he co-founded student protest group Scholarism amid a public outcry against a proposed patriotic education curriculum.

The following year, Scholarism activists occupied the forecourt outside Hong Kong government headquarters and staged a hunger strike to protest what they described as a “brainwashing” curriculum. In a widely reported encounter, the teenager Wong twice refused to shake hands with then-city leader Leung Chun-ying, who visited the protest site alongside education officials.
Hundreds of thousands of people rallied behind Wong and his fellow student activists, forcing the government to back down and shelve the proposal.

But the teenage campaigner was also viewed as somewhat distant and domineering among the inner circle of Scholarism. Lee, who mainly handled protest logistics at that time, described his relationship with Wong as “almost like that of a boss and subordinate.”

Chin, who joined Scholarism around 2013, similarly described Wong as a deeply rational figure who seldom expressed his emotions. “Ten years ago, everyone described him as someone without many feelings,” she said. “Like a robot.”
Wong might even come across as “rude,” she added, noting that he rarely said thanks to others during that period.

A large part of Wong’s youth coincided with a period of escalating social movements in Hong Kong. Just two years after the anti-patriotic education protests, the city saw the 79-day Umbrella Movement in 2014. Wong, then aged 17, took centre stage in mobilising public support for student protesters, who demanded democratic reform and universal suffrage.

In a demonstration that sparked the Umbrella Movement, Wong and other student leaders led protesters into the forecourt of the government headquarters in an action dubbed “Reclaiming Civic Square,” seeking to escalate their campaign. That eventually resulted in Wong’s first criminal conviction.

In 2016, Wong and fellow student leaders Alex Chow and Nathan Law were found guilty of unlawful assembly. Though initially spared prison, Wong later served around 69 days behind bars – his first jail term – following a government appeal in 2017. His penalty was ultimately quashed by the Court of Final Appeal in 2018.

Scholarism disbanded in 2016. Wong and several former members, as well as young activists like Law, went on to establish Demosisto, a political party advocating for “democratic self-determination” in the city. Wong served as general secretary.
Lee and Chin did not join the new party, and they grew estranged from Wong during that period.

That year, Law was elected to the Legislative Council, making him the youngest lawmaker in Hong Kong history at the age of 23. He won over 50,000 votes, giving Demosisto a strong popular mandate. The prospect of youth democracy activism appeared bright at the time, but Law was eventually disqualified from his seat in 2017 following an oath-taking controversy.
From left: Joshua Wong, Agnes Chow, and Nathan Law, photographed on March 10, 2018. Photo via HKFP. Used with permission.
Reconnections
It was only after Wong’s detention in late 2020 that Lee and Chin reconnected with him, beginning with an exchange of letters.

In 2019, citywide protests and unrest triggered by a controversial extradition bill engulfed the city. Wong and Demosisto were heavily involved in the protests, with the activist frequently lobbying foreign governments to impose sanctions on Hong Kong officials and halt the export of crowd control equipment to the city’s police force.

Then, in June 2020, Beijing imposed the national security law, effectively crushing political dissent in the city. Demosisto disbanded on the eve of the law’s enactment, while Nathan Law left Hong Kong in self-exile.
Written by Hong Kong Free Press
7afe3ce88c6c477c: KUALA LUMPUR, Nov 18 — Retirement preparedness in Malaysia may have less to do with income levels and more to do with the financial habits, behaviours and support systems people develop throughout their lives, according to research by Universiti Sains Malaysia, commissioned by FWD Malaysia (FWD). While rising living costs remain a significant challenge for many households, the study found that factors such as financial literacy, long-term planning and social influence play a critical role in determining retirement readiness across both lower- and middle-income segments. The research also found that only 12.5 per cent of retirees surveyed had high levels of financial resources, highlighting the financial vulnerabilities many Malaysians face as they approach retirement. The findings challenge the common perception that retirement security is primarily determined by earnings. Instead, they suggest that the ability to make informed financial decisions, build positive financial habits and stay committed to long-term goals may be equally important in shaping financial outcomes later in life. For many Malaysians, however, long-term planning often takes a back seat to more immediate financial concerns. Rising household expenses, family commitments and economic uncertainty can make retirement feel like a distant priority. “Our research shows that retirement preparedness is ultimately a lifelong journey,” said Mak See Sen, chief executive officer of FWD Insurance Berhad. “Income is important, but what often makes the difference is whether people have the confidence, financial knowledge and support to make good decisions consistently over time. That’s why we believe financial literacy should start early, long before retirement becomes a concern.” The study also highlighted growing vulnerabilities among Malaysia’s middle-income population. Despite relatively stable earnings, many M40 households face competing financial demands, including housing commitments, children’s education expenses and the responsibility of supporting ageing parents. Among retirees surveyed, nearly 60 per cent reported living with one or more major physical illnesses such as heart disease, diabetes, arthritis or hypertension, underscoring the additional financial pressures associated with ageing. Often referred to as the “sandwich generation”, many working adults find themselves balancing multiple responsibilities while trying to build their own financial security. According to FWD, these challenges often stem from financial behaviours and decisions formed earlier in life. As a result, improving retirement outcomes requires intervention long before individuals reach their peak earning years. To address this, FWD has invested RM5 million in a long-term financial literacy ecosystem designed to support Malaysians from childhood through young adulthood. Through programmes aimed at primary school, secondary school and university students, the initiative has reached more than 12,000 participants nationwide, particularly youths from low-income and financially vulnerable backgrounds. These efforts include FWD’s long-standing collaboration with Junior Achievement (JA) Malaysia, which equips students with essential financial literacy and entrepreneurship skills through experiential learning programmes. In addition to its school and university-based initiatives, FWD also partners with Junior Achievement (JA) Malaysia to equip young Malaysians with practical financial literacy and entrepreneurship skills. Through this collaboration, students gain exposure to real-world financial concepts and hands-on learning experiences that help build confidence in managing their financial future. Research findings also point to the importance of social influence in shaping financial behaviour. Family members, friends, mentors and community networks often play a significant role in determining how people approach money and long-term planning. The study further found that approximately one-third of retirees exhibited signs of cognitive challenges including forgetfulness, reinforcing the importance of building financial confidence and resilience earlier in life. Recognising this, FWD has focused on community-based partnerships that encourage peer-to-peer learning and support. Through its collaboration with ARUS Academy under the Fun(d) for Life: University Edition programme, participants are encouraged to apply their learning and share it within their own communities. “As Malaysia moves towards an ageing society, we need to help people build resilience long before they encounter financial difficulties. Financial literacy is not just about understanding money. It is about creating the confidence and capability to make choices that lead to greater security, independence and peace of mind.” Mak adds. FWD believes insurers and takaful operators have an important role to play beyond providing protection products. By investing in education, community empowerment and financial confidence-building, organisations can contribute to stronger long-term financial outcomes for future generations of Malaysians.
d1c0f3f0d45e2a5b: United Launch Alliance (ULA) says poor booster performance appears to have doomed Sunday's Vulcan mission, which lost an Amazon Leo satellite payload on the rocket's return to flight.

ULA's initial assessment points to trouble almost immediately. "Early indications are that just after liftoff the launch vehicle experienced low booster performance," it said. As a result, stage separation occurred at too low an altitude, and the rocket was not traveling fast enough for the payload to reach orbit.

The second stage appeared to perform well, with its RL10 engines operating as planned, but that wasn't enough to make up for the shortfall, and the mission failed. ULA lost telemetry approximately ten minutes into flight.

An investigation is underway, led by ULA and overseen by the US Federal Aviation Administration (FAA), which had to activate two Debris Response Areas where debris was falling. The agency directs aircraft to leave these areas, and others are prevented from entering.

Late Wednesday afternoon GMT, ULA posted an update stating that it looks like it might be the fuel supply rather than the BE-4 engines that caused the underperformance of the booster. The company wrote: “Preliminary indications are that the low booster thrust was the result of inadequate fuel supply from the vehicle to the BE-4 engines, not from the performance of the engines."

Previous flights had been blighted by problems with the solid rocket boosters, designed to give the rocket a kick at launch. Those issues prompted a stand-down while investigators examined the cause. This time, ULA said: "All indications are that the solid rocket booster performance was nominal, following nozzle improvements implemented for this launch."

Attention therefore turns to Vulcan's liquid-fueled core stage, powered by two Blue Origin BE-4 engines, though that does not establish an engine fault. Fuel delivery or another first-stage system could also be responsible, and the investigation is ongoing.

The BE-4 also powers Blue Origin's New Glenn rocket, which exploded on the launchpad during a ground test in May. In August, Blue Origin boss Dave Limp said that the issue originated at the main oxygen valve on one of the BE-4 engines. Modifications were made to deal with the problem.

The upper stage's apparently normal performance may offer some reassurance to NASA, although the investigation remains at an early stage. The agency dropped the delayed Exploration Upper Stage earlier this year and is pursuing a stretched Centaur V alongside its existing interim cryogenic propulsion stage as options for Artemis IV.
NASA is targeting Artemis IV for early 2028 and Artemis V for later that year.
ULA said: "We truly understand the impact this has on our customers and are committed to returning to flight as safely and quickly as we can."

The failure also dents ULA's otherwise impressive launch record. A predecessor of Vulcan, the Atlas V, has a 100 percent success record for payloads reaching orbit. However, it uses Russian RD-180 engines, a dependency the US wishes to remove. ®
Updated at 1747 GMT to reflect ULA's statement about the likely cause of the failure.
792da3987dfe9eae: China is hosting the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) summit for the third time in the past 25 years. The gathering in Shenzhen will see the leaders of the US, China and Russia sit down together for a formal three-way meeting for the first time in history. But what does China want from the summit? I see it as having three main priorities. First is to consolidate its position as one of the world’s most important diplomatic hubs. Second is to set out its vision for a new global order. And third is to take advantage of favourable geopolitical conditions, primarily brought about by US setbacks in Iran and Russia’s quagmire in Ukraine, to adjust the terms of its engagement with Washington and Moscow. 1. A diplomatic hub Hosting national leaders and other high-level officials has become a key feature of Chinese diplomacy in recent years. President Xi Jinping has welcomed over 25 world leaders to China so far in 2026. These include Canada’s Mark Carney, Germany’s Friedrich Merz, Spain’s Pedro Sánchez and the UK’s former prime minister, Keir Starmer. Beijing’s push to become a key diplomatic convener is a notable break from earlier forms of Chinese diplomacy. In the 2010s, the assertive and confrontational approach of Chinese officials on the international stage was widely known as “wolf warrior” diplomacy. The name is derived from a series of patriotic Chinese action films, also called Wolf Warrior. In this period, Chinese officials used social media to share controversial political memes and spar with foreign politicians and critical journalists, drawing condemnation in diplomatic circles. This belligerent approach was retired in the early 2020s. Notable wolf warriors such as China’s former foreign affairs minister Qin Gang and ministry spokesman Zhao Lijian were reassigned or removed from their posts. China’s hosting of the latest Apec summit is in line with Beijing’s new diplomatic strategy, suggesting it has acknowledged the limitations of the wolf warrior approach. 2. Reshaping the global order As well as showcasing China’s shifting approach to diplomacy, hosting major international events such as the Apec summit is a central part of Beijing’s wider ambitions to reshape the global order – most notably as a venue to gain greater legitimacy for its vision. This vision was summarised in a 45-page white paper released by China’s state council in June. The paper signalled the Chinese government’s desire to evolve from being a participant of the existing international system to the architect of a new global order where China and the global south play a greater role. The same message was repeated in the run-up to the Shenzhen summit. In a speech in late October, China’s foreign affairs minister Wang Yi declared that “the rise of the global south is the most momentous shift since the second world war”. He framed China’s hosting of multilateral events such as Apec as a vehicle to give developing countries a greater voice on the international stage. It is this vision that China seeks to convey to the wider world through the Shenzhen summit. 3. Great-power engagement The timing of the Shenzhen summit works in China’s favour. With the US and Russia currently bogged down in costly military conflicts in Iran and Ukraine respectively, and Trump reeling from a punishing electoral defeat, it is Xi who holds the strongest geopolitical hand. When Trump, Putin and Xi sit down together in Shenzhen on November 19, China may be in a position to push harder on the terms of its engagement with Washington and Moscow. A primary goal for China is to stabilise the global economy, which has been disrupted by the war in Iran. However, many commentators remain sceptical that the three-way meeting will deliver any concrete outcomes. The US and China recently extended their fragile trade truce, delaying the expiry date until January 2027. Preventing relations from deteriorating is thus probably in the interests of both countries. And on various other issues, the three leaders are entering the meeting with vastly different ambitions. Trump is focused primarily on agreeing a three-way nuclear arms control agreement. But China has historically refused to discuss any limitations on its nuclear arsenal while its stockpile of warheads remains smaller than the US and Russia’s. On the other hand, Russia has pushed to make Ukraine a central part of the talks. It is aiming to build support for a settlement to the war on terms favourable to Moscow. However, China has sought to keep Ukraine off the agenda entirely, fearing political backlash and deeper economic countermeasures from the EU should it back such a settlement. Regardless of this, the 2026 Apec summit offers a window into what China hopes to achieve on the international stage as well as the world it perceives itself to be in. Tom Harper does not work for, consult, own shares in or receive funding from any company or organisation that would benefit from this article, and has disclosed no relevant affiliations beyond their academic appointment.

088840b2862670e5: PUTRAJAYA, Nov 18 — The Court of Appeal today reserved its decision on businessman Tan Sri Tan Kok Ping’s appeal against a High Court ruling ordering him to pay RM350,000 in damages to Penang Chief Minister Chow Kon Yeow for defamation. A three-member panel comprising Justices Datuk Azizul Azmi Adnan, Datuk Aliza Sulaiman and Datuk Seri Latifah Mohd Tahar reserved its decision after hearing submissions from Tan’s counsel, Datuk K. Kirubakaran, and Chow’s counsel, K. Simon Murali. On December 3, 2024, the Penang High Court ordered Tan to pay RM350,000 in damages after finding that remarks he made at a press conference on October 18, 2023, were defamatory. The remarks, made in Mandarin, were translated as “incompetent”, “ignorant” and “shameless”. High Court judge Datuk Quay Chew Soon found that the remarks, which were published by six Chinese-language newspapers and an English-language daily, had seriously damaged Chow’s reputation. In his submissions before the Court of Appeal today, Kirubakaran argued that the High Court judge had erred in law and fact in finding the three words defamatory. He said Chow had merely stated the Malay translations of the three words as their alleged defamatory meanings in his statement of claim. However, in his witness statement, Chow had expanded on the meanings, attributing to the remarks a more injurious defamatory meaning than that originally pleaded. Kirubakaran argued that Chow could not rely on a more defamatory meaning than the one set out in his statement of claim, as doing so would be prejudicial to Tan. He added that Chow should be bound by his pleadings. He further submitted that the High Court judge had erred in accepting Chow’s self-serving explanation of the impugned remarks. “There was an absence of evidence from members of the community or third parties or experts on Chinese language as to the meaning and effect of the impugned statement on Chow,” he said. In response, Simon Murali urged the Court of Appeal to dismiss Tan’s appeal, submitting that the High Court’s judgment was beyond reproach and contained no appealable errors. He further submitted that the High Court judge had correctly considered the relevant facts and applied the applicable legal principles in finding that Tan was motivated by malice in making the defamatory remarks. Simon Murali said there was no appealable error in the High Court judge’s finding that Tan’s defence of justification was unsustainable. He added that the High Court had also rightly rejected Tan’s defences of qualified privilege and fair comment. Chow filed the defamation suit against Tan, who is the life honorary president of the Penang Chinese Chamber of Commerce, in January 2024 over remarks made by Tan concerning the sale of state land in Batu Kawan. At today’s Court of Appeal proceedings, Chow was represented by lawyers Kek Boon Wei, Lee Wen Qian, Fatimatuz Zahra Suhaimi and S. Sharanya. — Bernama

7f054a92225181ea: The Home Office has awarded a contract worth £178 million to a public-private hosting services joint venture - without competition - to support critical national infrastructure.

According to a notice published last week, Crown Hosting Data Centres (CHDC) won the seven-year contract to support "essential national infrastructure underpinning the Home Office's most critical systems, including border security, the Police National Computer (PNC), and core intelligence environments."

CHDC is a joint venture between the Cabinet Office, which owns 25 percent, and Ark Data Centres Ltd, which owns the rest. It was set up in 2015 for the express purpose of providing hosting services for the government.
The award was made through an existing framework agreement, set up in February 2022, awarded to CHDC without competition via a Voluntary Ex-Ante Transparency Notice.
The service is set to support Critical National Infrastructure, although the notice does not reveal specific services requested.

Mention of continued support for the Police National Computer may raise eyebrows. The Home Office is managing the transition of the aging legacy system to the Law Enforcement Data Service (LEDS) under the National Law Enforcement Data Program (NLEDP).

A notice in December 2024 said that the Home Office was "focused on the development and adoption of LEDS products to replace existing PNC capability across all police forces and other non-policing PNC consumers, enabling the retirement by March 2026 (the point at which PNC support will expire)." The government had previously set a target of decommissioning the PNC in 2022.
The Register has asked the Home Office to clarify why Crown Hosting support is necessary beyond this date.
The PNC – which is based on mainframe technology dating from the 1970s – was at the center of a scandal in 2021 when a technology failure led to the loss of 413,000 records of evidence.

The incident, which left then Prime Minister Boris Johnson floundering in Parliament, was the result of a scripting error in code designed to weed out records to be deleted from the PNC, a system running on a Fujitsu BS2000/OSD SE700-30 mainframe-based at a datacenter in Hendon, London.
In 2022, the Cabinet Office awarded a contract worth up to £250 million to CHDC, also without outside competition. ®

03692ec60cac1bbf: In a lab near Newark Airport in New Jersey, a team of around 30 experienced human sniffers are slowly working their way through every odor on Earth. Their careful notes—“nutty,” “peachy,” “marine”—are cross-referenced with a chemical analysis to create a rich set of training data for what AI startup Osmo calls the world’s first foundation model for smell. The company’s goal, says founder Alex Wiltschko, is “to give computers a sense of smell.”

“Scent molecules are really the only language most species on this planet can speak,” he says. “Most species can’t communicate with sound or visually, so it truly is Earth’s original language. And it’s incredibly powerful for us, from a memory and an emotional standpoint. You can smell something once and remember it for the rest of your life. You can smell something on the street and be pulled back to high school.”

In the last few months, Wiltschko claims, Osmo’s model has achieved “human-level olfactory intelligence.” The company’s definition of this is that the model is about as good as the average person at detecting and discriminating between smells, and about as good as a junior perfume designer at creating them. It says its technology is already being used in the fragrance industry to help brands design and manufacture new scents. Last month, the company says, Osmo’s AI model outperformed in-house perfumers at one of the world’s largest consumer goods companies. Wiltschko believes it could be deployed eventually for threat detection at airports, for example, or diagnosing diseases.

Wiltschko spun the startup out of his work at Google Brain, the search giant’s former AI research lab, in 2023, and he is running the same playbook as AI startups in other domains: Throw a lot of data at difficult problems, and see what happens. The challenge with scent, Wiltschko says, is that there was a dearth of good data. Before Osmo, there were fewer than 200,000 human descriptions of smells in existing databases, by his count. Plus, the chemical sensor devices needed to collect data are expensive, and the fragrance industry is secretive about its work on olfactory science.

A lot of the company’s work has been in creating its own dataset of more than 10 million human labels and 800 million “scent tokens,” which describe the exact molecules and concentrations that go into creating specific odors. Osmo uses spectrometers and other chemical sensors, running around the clock, to break down the molecular makeup of everything from fruit and flowers to pantry staples and organs. A team of around 70 trained data labelers in the US and overseas spend their days sniffing things and writing down what they smell like, using a standardized fragrance vocabulary.

Mapping out scents in this way is throwing out some unlikely parallels. In the same way that changing the order of words can drastically influence the meaning of a sentence, rearranging scent molecules in different proportions can drastically alter the smells humans perceive. “The scent tokens that define the smell of a newborn baby have massive overlap with the scent tokens in a fresh plate of cooked spaghetti,” Wiltschko says. (Specifically Barilla brand spaghetti, he says, which perhaps raises some questions for the people at the pasta factory.)

The company also creates its own scents, using a smell-printing robot the size of a school bus that mixes ingredients according to precise formulas to make samples for Osmo’s own research and fragrances for paying customers. It can design and print scents to order based on a ChatGPT-style prompt. Wiltschko flipped open his laptop to show me how the AI model worked. He opened a text box on screen, and I asked him to generate a fragrance that smelled like a Portuguese custard tart (we were in Lisbon for Web Summit), aimed at 18- to 23-year-old men. The system spent a few minutes cogitating, then generated three options for potential scent profiles that matched the brief (creamy, coconutty, fruity) and the molecules needed to create them. If I’d continued with the ordering process, my signature L’Eau de Custard would have been ready about a week later.

Osmo’s technology has already been used to create retail fragrances, including for giants like Procter & Gamble. The Gates Foundation, which invested $5 million when Osmo launched, later gave the company a $3.5 million grant to assess molecules that repel disease-carrying insects, and Osmo identified eight substances that were more repellent than DEET. Osmo has also worked with StockX, the online clothing marketplace, on using smell to spot counterfeit sneakers by detecting differences in the chemical composition of the materials used in the shoes.

But not everyone is convinced by the technology or the company’s big claims. Avery Gilbert, a smell scientist and author of What the Nose Knows, has been sharply critical of Osmo on his Substack, arguing that some of its marketing claims are undocumented, and that its patent filings still rely on human sensory panels and perfumers, rather than AI. “This heavy reliance on human sensory judgments seems odd for a company premised on super-cool AI,” he wrote in March. A representative for Osmo did not respond in time for publication.

Michael Schmuker, a former professor of neural computation at the University of Hertfordshire who has previously consulted for Osmo, says the company’s technology is an achievement. With colleagues, he created an open-source, reverse-engineered version of Osmo’s 2023 model, but it lacks the reams of data the company has collected since.

But even with all this smell data, Osmo may be missing some of the factors that make human olfaction unique, Schmuker says. “Smell is super complex. Context is very important for smell. The same molecule may evoke a different association depending on context,” he says. “[The smell of] a French cheese like Camembert is partly the same molecule as in used nappies. You don’t confuse the two because of the context.”

In a controlled setting like a fragrance lab, this lack of context may not matter so much. But it could have an impact if Osmo’s technology becomes, as Wiltschko suggests, the “olfactive channel” for AI world models. Imagine a machine that could sniff out spoilage in food on a production line, or detect tumors through smell the way dogs have been trained to do in pilot studies.
For that to happen, sensor technology will need to get a lot better, Schmuker says. The models will need to keep improving. Medical diagnostics is the biggest prize.

“There’s a lot of history of companies that have gone directly at that mountain peak and, unfortunately, not been successful, because it is very expensive and it is very difficult,” Wiltschko says. “So what we’re doing is building this foundation at the foothills of all these mountains. We’re sending expeditions up to the mountains, doing explorations, and basically smelling the whole world.”

He said the victim, who testified as the second prosecution witness (SP2), had given clear and detailed evidence, which was further supported by her prompt disclosure to her mother (SP1) on the day of the incident. “We do not consider the discrepancy concerning SP2’s position when SP4, the victim’s schoolmate, entered the room to be sufficiently material to undermine the credibility of her testimony,” he said. On March 19, 2025, the Muar Sessions Court acquitted and discharged Ahnaf Afiq of the charges at the close of the defence case. However, the Muar High Court subsequently allowed the prosecution’s appeal, set aside the acquittal, convicted the accused and imposed a sentence of four years’ imprisonment and two strokes of the cane for the offence under Section 14(a). The Court further imposed an additional sentence of two years’ imprisonment and two strokes of the cane for the offence under Section 16(1), to take effect consecutively upon completion of the sentence imposed under Section 14(a). Ahnaf Afiq was charged with sexually assaulting an eight-year-old girl in the workroom of the library at a primary school in Muar, between 10.20 am and 11.20 am on October 3, 2019. 0bbe03ed3a7069de: SAP's commercial terms could put its latest AI tools out of reach for many customers, particularly smaller businesses running a single ERP system, the new chair of its German-speaking user group has warned.

Thomas Henzler, appointed chair of DSAG last month, told The Register that Joule Studio 2.0 – SAP's upgraded platform for developing and deploying AI agents to automate business tasks – is a leap forward.
Yet DSAG, which represents SAP users in Germany, Switzerland, and Austria, remains in talks with the vendor about the commercial conditions attached to access.

In July 2023, CEO Christian Klein told investors that SAP's "newest innovations and capabilities" will only be delivered in the public or private cloud using RISE with SAP, the vendor's lift-shift-and-transform program launched with partners and cloud providers in early 2021. Customers running ERP software on-premises, or hosting it with a hyperscaler outside RISE, will miss out, he said.

However, in May this year, SAP appeared to perform a U-turn. It said on-premises customers could access Joule 2.0 if they commit to a cloud "journey" through RISE with SAP, changing their support and commercial arrangements while migration projects are still underway.

Henzler told The Reg: "There is a gap between the customer's reality and SAP's strategy for the autonomous enterprise. A lot of customers are still planning to migrate to S/4HANA, and now the question is, 'what do we have to do to use SAP AI, and what does it mean regarding the cloud strategy?'

"Now it's a completely new strategy, a new approach, and a new underlying technology. The question is, what does it mean for existing projects, S/4HANA migrations, cloud migrations and so on? Is it necessary to rethink all the projects? Is there a big shift in the technology and architectures?"
The DSAG chair said the biggest challenge in connecting legacy on-prem systems, such as ECC, to the new Joule suite is the commercial model.

"Access requires a substantial RISE commitment and a minimum cloud-to-on-premise maintenance ratio. In practice, this creates a problem for customers with only one ECC system. To meet the cloud threshold, they have to convert their entire on-premises maintenance into a cloud subscription, which defeats the purpose of an on-premises connector. Consequently, the model only works for large enterprises with multiple SAP ERP systems that can, for example, migrate one system after the other to unlock AI for the rest," he said.

"In the end, to get the benefit you have to start a RISE with SAP migration. Therefore, the connector doesn't make sense for the majority of SME customers. From my perspective, this approach works only for large customers with multiple ERP systems, for example, if they take one system, move it to the cloud, and then another one. Then they can use AI, because they reach the needed ratio to use the on-prem connector. That is more or less a commercial approach. We need a solution for all customers, independent of the commercials."

The Register asked SAP to respond to Henzler's concerns. A spokesperson said: "The offering separates a customer's commercial commitment to cloud ERP from the timing of its operational migration. Customers that meet the applicable commercial and technical requirements can use supported AI capabilities with eligible ECC or on-premises SAP S/4HANA systems while modernizing their landscape. Eligibility is not determined by the number of ERP instances and can therefore also extend to single-instance customers."

There are thousands of SAP ERP users worldwide, including some of the world's largest businesses. Despite efforts to get them onto the latest iteration – S/4HANA – and in the cloud, where the vendor promised it could gather a greater "share of wallet" from customers, there has been a dogged resistance to these complex and time-consuming migrations.

Gartner figures for Q4 2024 showed only 39 percent of worldwide ECC customers – from a total of 35,000 – had bought or subscribed to SAP S/4HANA licenses. More recently, The Reg uncovered that SAP was about €2 billion short of its target for getting customers off on-prem support.
Customers still running older ERP systems face pressure to embrace AI-supported automation. Whether SAP's terms help them do that – or simply help move them onto RISE – remains the question. ®
f782436b47c7ae83: RIYADH، Nov 18 — A powerful explosion rattled homes in Riyadh on Wednesday، AFP journalists and residents said، as Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthis pressed their campaign of attacks against the kingdom. The location of the explosion was not immediately clear، but residents told AFP they saw smoke near Riyadh’s airport in the northeast of the city. In October، a deadly attack targeting Riyadh’s King Khalid International Airport killed 14 people and injured hundreds، forcing the suspension of flights for two weeks. Within minutes، the Saudi-led coalition fighting the Houthis said its air defences had intercepted and destroyed a cruise missile launched by the group towards the Riyadh region. Earlier، the coalition had reported intercepting another cruise missile also heading for the same region. Saudi civil defence authorities also said they had activated early warning systems in the southern regions of Jazan، Najran and Khamis Mushait، near the Yemeni border. The Saudi-led coalition، which backs neighbouring Yemen’s internationally recognised government in its war with the Houthis، has battled a surge in attacks since hostilities reignited in July. The long-running civil war in Yemen، one of the world’s poorest countries، had been largely dormant after a ceasefire went into effect in 2022. The Houthis are now nearing Aden، the government’s interim capital، having made sweeping territorial gains since the war resumed. Since the summer، more than 1,600 people have been killed and over 300,000 displaced by the fighting، according to the United Nations. — AFP
